In mathematics, a '''locally profinite group''' is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[topological group]] in which every [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighborhood]] of the identity element contains a [[compact space|compact]] open subgroup. Equivalently, a locally profinite group is a topological group that is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], [[Locally compact space|locally compact]], and [[totally disconnected group|totally disconnected]]. Moreover, a locally profinite group is compact if and only if it is [[profinite group|profinite]]; this explains the terminology. Basic examples of locally profinite groups are [[discrete group]]s and the [[p-adic Lie group|''p''-adic Lie group]]s. Non-examples are real [[Lie group]]s, which have the [[no small subgroup property]].

In a locally profinite group, a closed subgroup is locally profinite, and every compact subgroup is contained in an open compact subgroup.

== Examples ==
Important examples of locally profinite groups come from [[algebraic number theory]]. Let ''F'' be a [[Non-Archimedean ordered field|non-archimedean]] [[local field]]. Then both ''F'' and <math>F^\times</math> are locally profinite. More generally, the matrix ring <math>\operatorname{M}_n(F)</math> and the [[general linear group]] <math>\operatorname{GL}_n(F)</math> are locally profinite. Another example of a locally profinite group is the absolute [[Weil group]] of a non-archimedean local field: this is in contrast to the fact that the [[absolute Galois group]] of such is profinite (in particular compact).

== Representations of a locally profinite group ==
Let ''G'' be a locally profinite group. Then a group homomorphism <math>\psi: G \to \mathbb{C}^\times</math> is continuous if and only if it has open kernel. 

Let <math>(\rho, V)</math> be a complex representation of ''G''.<ref>We do not put a topology on ''V''; so there is no topological condition on the representation.</ref> <math>\rho</math> is said to be [[smooth representation|smooth]] if ''V'' is a union of <math>V^K</math> where ''K'' runs over all open compact subgroups ''K''. <math>\rho</math> is said to be [[admissible representation|admissible]] if it is smooth and <math>V^K</math> is finite-dimensional for any open compact subgroup ''K''.

We now make a blanket assumption that <math>G/K</math> is at most countable for all open compact subgroups ''K''.

The dual space <math>V^*</math> carries the [[group action|action]] <math>\rho^*</math> of ''G'' given by <math>\left\langle \rho^*(g) \alpha, v \right\rangle = \left\langle \alpha, \rho^*(g^{-1}) v \right\rangle</math>. In general, <math>\rho^*</math> is not smooth. Thus, we set <math>\widetilde{V} = \bigcup_K (V^*)^K</math> where <math>K</math> is acting through <math>\rho^*</math> and set <math>\widetilde{\rho} = \rho^*</math>. The smooth representation <math>(\widetilde{\rho}, \widetilde{V})</math> is then called the [[contragredient representation|contragredient]] or smooth dual of <math>(\rho, V)</math>.

The contravariant [[functor]]
:<math>(\rho, V) \mapsto (\widetilde{\rho}, \widetilde{V})</math>
from the category of smooth representations of ''G'' to itself is exact. Moreover, the following are equivalent.
* <math>\rho</math> is admissible.
* <math>\widetilde{\rho}</math> is admissible.<ref>Blondel, Corollary 2.8.</ref>
* The canonical ''G''-module map <math>\rho \to \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho}}</math> is an isomorphism.
When <math>\rho</math> is admissible, <math>\rho</math> is irreducible if and only if <math>\widetilde{\rho}</math> is irreducible. 

The countability assumption at the beginning is really necessary, for there exists a locally profinite group that admits an irreducible smooth representation <math>\rho</math> such that <math>\widetilde{\rho}</math> is not irreducible.

== Hecke algebra of a locally profinite group ==
:{{see also|Hecke algebra of a locally compact group}}

Let <math>G</math> be a unimodular locally profinite group such that <math>G/K</math> is at most countable for all open compact subgroups ''K'', and  <math>\mu</math> a left Haar measure on <math>G</math>. Let <math>C^\infty_c(G)</math> denote the space of locally constant functions on <math>G</math> with compact support. With the multiplicative structure given by
:<math>(f * h)(x) = \int_G f(g) h(g^{-1} x) d \mu(g)</math>
<math>C^\infty_c(G)</math> becomes not necessarily unital associative <math>\mathbb{C}</math>-algebra. It is called the Hecke algebra of ''G'' and is denoted by <math>\mathfrak{H}(G)</math>. The algebra plays an important role in the study of smooth representations of locally profinite groups. Indeed, one has the following: given a smooth representation <math>(\rho, V)</math> of ''G'', we define a new action on ''V'':
:<math>\rho(f) = \int_G f(g) \rho(g) d\mu(g).</math>
Thus, we have the functor <math>\rho \mapsto \rho</math> from the category of smooth representations of <math>G</math> to the category of non-degenerate <math>\mathfrak{H}(G)</math>-modules. Here, "non-degenerate" means <math>\rho(\mathfrak{H}(G))V=V</math>. Then the fact is that the functor is an [[Equivalence of categories|equivalence]].<ref>Blondel, Proposition 2.16.</ref>
